t.2.69.1: Kausalyā, recognizing the voice of the great-souled Bharata as he cried out in this way, spoke these words to Sumitrā.
t.2.69.3: Having spoken thus to Sumitrā, she, pale and clad in soiled garments, trembling and bereft of her senses, set out for the place where Bharata was.
t.2.69.2: Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī of cruel deeds, has come. I wish to see that far-sighted Bharata.
t.2.69.4: Then Bharata, the younger brother of Rāma, accompanied by Śatrughna, set out for the place where Kausalyā's dwelling stood.
t.2.69.5: Then Śatrughna and Bharata, themselves grief-stricken, seeing Kausalyā fallen down, afflicted with sorrow and bereft of consciousness, embraced her.
t.2.69.6: Kausalyā, deeply grieved, replied to Bharata thus: "Here is the kingdom you desired, obtained by you free of all thorns; alas, Kaikeyī has secured it swiftly through a cruel deed!"
t.2.69.7: Having sent my son away clad in bark garments to dwell in the forest, what advantage does cruel-eyed Kaikeyī see in that?
t.2.69.8: Kaikeyī ought quickly to send me away as well, to the place where my son of very great fame, the golden-naveled one, now dwells.
t.2.69.9: Or else I myself, accompanied by Sumitrā, will gladly set out, placing the sacred fire of the agnihotra before me, to where Rāghava is.
t.2.69.10: Or rather, you yourself ought to take me there today, to the place where that tiger among men, my son, is practicing austerities.
t.2.69.12: Then Bharata, with palms joined in reverence, replied thus to Kausalyā, who was lamenting in this way, overwhelmed by many sorrows.
t.2.69.11: For this kingdom of yours, vast, abounding in wealth and grain, and filled with elephants, horses and chariots, has been handed over to you by her.
t.2.69.13: Noble lady, why do you reproach me, who knew nothing of this and am free from sin? You know well my deep and steadfast love for Rāghava.
t.2.69.14: May he never possess an understanding shaped in accordance with the scriptures, the man by whose consent the noble one, true to his promise and foremost among the virtuous, went away.
t.2.69.15: May the one with whose consent the noble one went away become a servant of the most wicked, may he urinate facing the sun, and may he kick a sleeping cow with his foot.
t.2.69.16: Whatever sin falls on a master who has his servant perform a great task and then leaves him unrewarded, let that sin be hers, the one with whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.17: The sin of those who act treacherously against a king who protects all beings as his own sons, may that sin fall upon him by whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.18: Whatever sin falls upon a king who takes a sixth share as tribute yet does not protect his subjects, may that sin be his by whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.19: Whatever sin belongs to those who, having promised the sacrificial fee to ascetics at a sattra, then falsely deny it, may that sin be his by whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.20: In a battle thronged with elephants, horses and chariots and teeming with weapons, may he with whose consent the noble one went away fail to uphold the dharma of the virtuous.
t.2.69.21: May that wicked-souled man, with whose consent the noble one went away, lose the scripture of most subtle meaning that a wise teacher taught him with great effort.
t.2.69.22: May that heartless man by whose consent the noble one went away eat rice-pudding, sesame-rice and goat's flesh for himself alone, and may he also show contempt for his elders.
t.2.69.23: Though surrounded in his own house by sons, wives and servants, may he eat his dainty food alone, he with whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.24: The sin that is said to lie in slaying a king, a woman, a child or an old man, and the sin that lies in abandoning one's dependents, may he incur that sin.
t.2.69.25: Whatever sin is reckoned to one who lies asleep through both twilights, may that sin be his by whose consent the noble one went away.
t.2.69.26: Whatever sin lies in one who sets fire to a house, whatever sin lies in one who defiles his guru's bed, and whatever sin lies in betraying a friend, may he incur that sin.
t.2.69.27: May the man with whose consent the noble one went away never render service to the gods, to the ancestors, or likewise to his mother and father.
t.2.69.29: Thus consoling Kausalyā, who had been bereft of husband and son, the king's son, stricken with grief, fell to the ground.
t.2.69.28: May he by whose consent the noble one went away fall swiftly, this very day, from the world of the virtuous, from the fame of the virtuous, and likewise from the deeds cherished by the good.
t.2.69.30: To Bharata, who was thus swearing terrible oaths, senseless and consumed by grief, Kausalyā spoke these words.
t.2.69.31: This sorrow of mine, my son, arises in me all the more, for by swearing these oaths you are stifling my very breath of life.
t.2.69.33: As the great-souled one, stricken with sorrow, lamented thus, his mind became agitated through bewilderment and the obstruction of his grief.
t.2.69.34: As he lamented again and again, senseless, his mind utterly lost, fallen upon the ground and sighing long and repeatedly, that night passed for him in grief.
t.2.69.32: By good fortune your self, together with Lakṣmaṇa, has not swerved from dharma. My child, true to your vow, you will attain the worlds of the virtuous.
